title: DeepSeek And Moonshot AI Models Appear To Carry Hidden NVIDIA Blackwell Fingerprints In Their Starting Weights, Pointing To Training Clusters Of 3,000 To 4,500 GPUs
summary: DeepSeek and Moonshot models carry hidden Nvidia Blackwell chip fingerprints
detailed: With chip tensions between the US and China experiencing another surge following former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the firm, forensic analysis conducted by Uemployment Labs suggests that several Chinese AI models might have relied on thousands of NVIDIA's latest Blackwell AI GPUs for their training run.

The data, which relies on matching the hardware imprint of each chip with the imprint generated via analyzing a model's weights, does, however, suggest that individual training runs utilized clusters ranging between 4,500 and 3,000 Blackwell GPUs, with combined multi-model footprints reaching upwards of 12,000 chips across participating labs.

DuPue claims to have compared the pattern of static weights in the AI models against the initialization patterns produced by the streaming multiprocessor (SM) layouts of NVIDIA’s Hopper and Blackwell GPUs to conclude that the models started their training runs with the NVIDIA chips.

The estimate ranges from 7,000 to 22,000 GPUs cumulatively for the DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the MiniMax-M3, Kimi K3 and the Ling-3.1-flash AI models and is highly dependent on the time of the training run, GPU usage efficiency and other factors.
sentences: With chip tensions between the US and China experiencing another surge following former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the firm, forensic analysis conducted by Uemployment Labs suggests that several Chinese AI models might have relied on thousands of NVIDIA's latest Blackwell AI GPUs for their training run.

The AI lab attempted to match hardware fingerprints linked specifically to the Blackwell chips by reverse engineering AI model weights and recovering the thread count for the processors that initialized the AI model's training run.

While Unemployment Labs' report claims to show that some Chinese labs were able to access the advanced Blackwell GPUs, it does add that the evidence is not to evaluate whether Blackwell gPU export control regulations were violated.

The data, which relies on matching the hardware imprint of each chip with the imprint generated via analyzing a model's weights, does, however, suggest that individual training runs utilized clusters ranging between 4,500 and 3,000 Blackwell GPUs, with combined multi-model footprints reaching upwards of 12,000 chips across participating labs.
The researchers analyzed the AI models' published weights and used these to figure out the seed that generated the initial model weights at the time DeepSeek and others started model training.
Model weights, also called parameters, enable an AI model to transform input into output.
Most weights transform throughout the training phase, but the initial set can be determined by some static weights, says Depue.
A seed is a value fed into a number generator to produce a set of numbers that are called initial weights.
The initial set of numbers is locked into a matrix pattern dependent on the AI GPU design architecture used at the time of training initialization.

DuPue claims to have compared the pattern of static weights in the AI models against the initialization patterns produced by the streaming multiprocessor (SM) layouts of NVIDIA’s Hopper and Blackwell GPUs to conclude that the models started their training runs with the NVIDIA chips.

Because each type of AI chip has a fixed number of processing cores, that hardware layout dictates the exact grid pattern used to place starting random numbers into an AI model before training begins.
Each GPU architecture has a different SM layout, which makes the GPU class identifiable if one looks deep enough at an AI model's weights.
By relying on pattern matching, the researchers conclude that several thousand Blackwell GPUs were used by DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Inclusion AI.

The estimate ranges from 7,000 to 22,000 GPUs cumulatively for the DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the MiniMax-M3, Kimi K3 and the Ling-3.1-flash AI models and is highly dependent on the time of the training run, GPU usage efficiency and other factors.
The 22,000 figure assumes that the models did not train on the same Blackwell Cluster.
It is quite modest, compared to, for instance, Elon Musk's plan to bring more than a million of such chips online by 2026 end.
Similarly, Commerce Department guidance issued in May this year stated that the restrictions also applied to selling to subsidiaries of Chinese companies typically located in Singapore or Malaysia.
The recent saga surrounding NVIDIA's founder and former CEO, Jensen Huang, has also brought fresh spotlight for chip exports to China.
Legislation in Congress seeks to target remote access while Chinese firms are already rushing to secure orders before the rules are further tightened.
NVIDIA's CUDA stack provides it a key advantage in the AI chip industry as it was the only mature GPU platform at the time deep learning grew in popularity.
However, some, such as Anthropic, have claimed that switching to AMD GPUs is now just a matter of weeks for some applications.
The trail also goes cold with the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, as the newest AI model from the Chinese lab has a new architecture.

This architecture masks the GPU initialization footprint, with Defue noting:
"Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them.

We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search."
